name: Sanganeri hand block printing
summary: Sanganeri hand block printing is a hand block-printed textile tradition of Sanganer town, about 16 km from Jaipur, registered as a Geographical Indication (application no. 147) by the Calico Printers Co-operative Society. It is known for fine, repetitive floral butis and butas on a white ground, printed by Chhipa printers with blocks carved by Kharadi block-makers, traditionally using a harda (myrobalan) pre-treatment, iron (syahi) and alum (begar) mordants dyed in alizarin/madder, sun-bleaching, dabu mud-resist and indigo. Since the 1960s the craft has faced competition from screen printing and a large shift to synthetic dyes, and the cluster is associated with documented water pollution.

concepts.title: Screen printing, synthetic dyes and revival (1960s onward)
concepts.summary: Screen printing entered Sanganer around 1960 through Khatri migrants from Mirpur and Sind, and many printing families adopted mill cloth, synthetic dyes and screens.
concepts.body_md:
Screen printing entered Sanganer around 1960 through Khatri migrants from Mirpur and Sind, and many printing families adopted mill cloth, synthetic dyes and screens. [S10]

Screen printing emerged in Sanganer in the 1960s as a cheaper, faster method using synthetic dyes, and some block printers also adopted synthetic dyes. [S12]

Over the preceding decades a large number of screen-printing units arose, and screen-printed 'Sanganeri' textiles were being sold across India. [S1]

The craft was revived in the 1970s with patrons including Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay and Anokhi; floods in 1981 set the industry back, and Sanganer joined a UNIDO cluster programme in 1997. [S10]

Gaatha says chemical dyes were introduced in the 1980s and widened the range of colours. [S8]
